text: Haw Par Villa: The Tiger Balm Garden of Statues

On a hill above Pasir Panjang Road stands the strangest garden in Singapore: a terraced hillside crowded with painted concrete statues — gods and demons, monkeys and mermaids, sinners being sawn in half — built by the Tiger Balm fortune as part gift, part advertisement and part moral textbook.
There the architect Ho Kwang Yew built an Art Deco villa, finished in 1937, which Boon Haw gave to his younger brother Boon Par.
It was also, quite deliberately, a school: its statues were meant to teach Chinese cultural values — filial piety, charity, loyalty, resistance to temptation, and what awaited the wicked after death.

Returning from Hong Kong, he rebuilt the garden and greatly enlarged it, adding sculptures in the spaces that had been the family's recreation ground — over the swimming pool, the tennis courts and the lawns.

The Courts are a walk-through of the underworld of Chinese Buddhist and Taoist belief, in which the dead are judged court by court by ten Yama kings, each presiding over punishments fitted to particular sins, before their next reincarnation is decided.

The virtuous cross the Golden Bridge to paradise; those whose good deeds outweigh their sins cross the Silver Bridge; the wicked are shown their own faces in the Mirror of Retribution and sent on to the courts below.

The result, reopened in 1990, was Haw Par Villa Dragon World — an 80 Singapore dollars-million theme park with an amphitheatre, theatres, and the Ten Courts of Hell rebuilt as a boat ride through the inside of a 60-metre-long dragon.
In 2001 the operator gave up its rights, the board took the park back, and Haw Par Villa became a free public park again, as it had been in the family's day.

That October came the boldest addition since Boon Haw's day: Hell's Museum, billed as the world's first museum dedicated to death and the afterlife — 3,800 square metres on how the world's religions and cultures treat death, with replicas of an altar, a burial crypt, a traditional Chinese grave and a void-deck funeral, wrapped around the Ten Courts, which now sit inside it.

Journeys' contract ended on the 7th of December 2025, and from the next day the Singapore Tourism Board closed the park partially, for essential maintenance and repair works, until further notice — saying the works were needed to ensure public safety while preserving the park's cultural and artistic elements, and that it was reviewing the future plans for Haw Par Villa.
